problem: Existing scene memories for embodied agents fall short in three ways. Object-centric 3D scene graphs such as ConceptGraphs reduce the scene to isolated objects with bounding boxes and textual relations, so they lose free-space and oriented spatial information (e.g. whether there is room 'in front of' an armchair). Dense point-cloud or neural-field maps are expensive, do not scale as the scene grows, and are poorly understood by current foundation models. Neither kind represents unexplored space, so neither supports active, lifelong exploration.
motivation: A single image already carries rich, robust information about a local region: objects, their spatial layout and room-level context. Modern VLMs reason over images far better than over 3D scene graphs or point clouds. So a compact set of well-chosen images can serve as a scalable, target-agnostic 3D memory that a VLM can use both to answer questions and to decide where to explore next.
key_idea: Represent explored space as a minimal set of 'Memory Snapshots', each an image chosen by co-visibility clustering to cover a cluster of co-visible objects. Represent unexplored space as 'Frontier Snapshots', images looking toward frontiers. A VLM then picks among these images either to answer or navigate, or to explore further, with LLM-based prefiltering to retrieve only relevant memory.
insight: Swapping only the memory format while keeping the exploration pipeline and prefiltering identical isolates the value of snapshot images over object crops. ConceptGraphs w/ Frontier Snapshots scores 47.2/33.3 (LLM-Match/SPL) against 52.6/42.0 for 3D-Mem on A-EQA, and 61.5/45.3 against 69.1/48.9 SR/SPL on GOAT-Bench. The gains concentrate on spatial-understanding questions (43.4 vs 32.9) and object localization (48.6 vs 32.1), where background and inter-object context matter. Letting the VLM choose among frontier snapshots, instead of going to the nearest frontier, is chiefly an efficiency win: A-EQA SPL drops from 42.0 to 31.0 without it (LLM-Match 52.6→49.3). Persistent memory matters in lifelong navigation: 'w/o memory' drops GOAT-Bench to 58.6/38.5 with GPT-4o and 40.6/14.6 with LLaVA-7B. Two further observations: re-deciding every 1 m beats committing to a target (50.5/36.2 on A-EQA), and image-goal SPL is below ConceptGraphs (44.2 vs 52.8), which exposes VLM weakness at cross-viewpoint image matching.
method: Object mapping: follows the ConceptGraphs pipeline (segmentation, 3D back-projection, matching/merging) with YOLOv8x-World and a 200-class ScanNet vocabulary. It maintains a global object set (category, confidence, 3D location) and frame candidates, each an RGB-D frame with its set of co-visible detected objects; only objects within max_dist=3.5 m are added.

Co-Visibility Clustering (Memory Snapshots): bisecting-style hierarchical clustering. It repeatedly takes the largest unsettled object cluster and looks for frames whose detected objects contain the whole cluster. If one exists, the frame with the most objects (ties broken by summed confidence) becomes that cluster's snapshot; otherwise the cluster is split in two by K-Means on 2D (x,y) positions. Snapshots sharing a frame are merged, giving a compact partition of all objects into images.

Frontier Snapshots: frontiers come from a 0.1 m voxel occupancy map. The explored region is navigable space within 1.7 m of the trajectory, frontiers are DBSCAN clusters of unexplored pixels (>20 pixels, split if spanning >150° of view), and each frontier stores a region, a navigable location and an image looking toward it. The image is re-captured when region IoU with the previous version falls below 0.95.

Incremental construction: at each step 3 egocentric views (60° apart) update the object set. Only objects seen at this step, plus the objects of the snapshots they already belong to, are re-clustered, and the new clusters replace those old snapshots. Frontiers are added, modified or removed.

Prefiltering (memory retrieval): the VLM receives the question and all object classes in memory and returns the top-K (K=10) relevant classes; snapshots containing none of them are dropped. On average about 3.3 of 10.9 snapshots remain on A-EQA and 4.7 of 16.6 on GOAT-Bench.

VLM decision and navigation: GPT-4o sees the egocentric views, the prefiltered memory snapshots (tagged with class names) and the frontier snapshots. For EQA it either picks a frontier with a rationale or picks a memory snapshot and answers. For GOAT-Bench object crops are appended per class and the VLM picks an object. The agent moves via the Habitat-sim pathfinder at most 1.0 m, or until within 0.5 m of the target, before re-deciding (max 50 steps).

Open-source variant: LLaVA-1.5-7B is LoRA fine-tuned jointly on exploration choice (loss weight 1) and prefiltering ranking (weight 0.3). Data are generated from GOAT-Bench train scenes (136 HM3D scenes, 3669 targets, about 4 shortest-path trajectories of ~12 steps per target) with GPT-4o-labelled prefilter rankings; snapshots are compressed to 3×3 tokens.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o via OpenAI API (frozen) for prefiltering and exploration/answer decisions, with YOLOv8x-World detector + ConceptGraphs-style object mapping. A GOAT-Bench variant uses LLaVA-1.5-7B (LoRA fine-tuned).
setting.training_data: none (training-free) for the main GPT-4o system. The LLaVA-7B variant is fine-tuned on self-generated trajectories from GOAT-Bench train exploration data (136 HM3D train scenes, 3669 target objects, ~4 paths/target × ~12 steps), with GPT-4o-generated prefiltering rankings.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D + precise pose; 3 views per step at 60° spacing (captured 1280×1280 for detection, resized to 360×360 for the VLM). The GOAT-Bench goal is given as category, language description, or image.
setting.action_space: high-level selection of a frontier snapshot or a memory snapshot/object; executed as point-goal motion with the Habitat-sim navmesh pathfinder (≤1.0 m per decision step, stop within 0.5 m; max 50 steps)
setting.simulator: Habitat (HM3D scenes) for A-EQA and GOAT-Bench; EM-EQA uses provided ScanNet/HM3D RGB-D trajectories offline
setting.privileged: GT agent pose required for mapping; Habitat-sim pathfinder using the global navmesh for low-level path planning (authors say it can be replaced by the occupancy-map planner). EM-EQA provides the full scan trajectory with poses (no exploration).

results: On the A-EQA 184-question subset, 3D-Mem (GPT-4o) reaches 52.6 LLM-Match and 42.0 LLM-Match SPL. This beats ConceptGraphs w/ Frontier Snapshots (47.2/33.3), Explore-EQA (46.9/23.4) and OpenEQA's Multi-Frame GPT-4o (41.8/7.5); on the full set it scores 53.3/38.0. On EM-EQA it gets 57.2 LLM-Match with ~3.1 frames, against Multi-Frame's 48.1 with 3.0 frames. On the GOAT-Bench Val Unseen subset it reaches 69.1 SR / 48.9 SPL, versus CG w/ Frontier Snapshots at 61.5/45.3, Explore-EQA at 55.0/37.9 and Modular GOAT at 24.9/17.2. It scores 62.9/44.7 on the whole set, and a fine-tuned LLaVA-7B variant gets 49.6/29.4.
limitations: Assumes static scenes and precise agent pose, and depends on object-detector quality: missed or mislabelled detections are a major failure source. The occupancy/frontier representation does not support multi-floor scenes, which hurts A-EQA.

Main comparisons use subsets (184 A-EQA questions, 36-scene/278-subtask GOAT-Bench subset) and a proprietary GPT-4o. Low-level motion uses Habitat's global navmesh pathfinder, and the 360×360 snapshot resolution limits small-object recognition.
Latency is noticeable: about 3.3–3.6 s VLM inference plus about 2.4–2.8 s 2D-3D lifting per step. The VLM also struggles with cross-viewpoint image matching (image-goal SPL is below ConceptGraphs).
